newsitem.title: CANADA: Manitoba Telecom shares start trading.
newsitem.headline: Manitoba Telecom shares start trading.

text.p: Shares in 90-year-old Manitoba Telecom Services Ltd, Canada's fifth largest telephone company, began trading on several Canadian exchanges on Tuesday to mixed reviews.
The C$910 million public issue of shares in Canada's second last government-owned telephone company was made in December exclusively to Manitoba residents at C$13 a share.
The 70 million share offer included 48.45 million shares represented by instalment receipts.
Manitoba Telecom common shares were at 13.70 on the Toronto Stock Exchange in turnover of 2.77 million shares in their first few hours of trading. They traded as high as 13.95 and as low as 13.65.

"I think they have certain challenges ahead of them, that there is usually a transition period for a newly privatized company to get in sync with investors. I think the stock is a hold," said Robert Harding, an analyst with Goepel Shields.
A company sold off by the government must adjust its accounting methods so they accord with those of other publicly held telephone companies.
It must break out operating results and offer segmented information. Manitoba Telecom must also keep a rein on costs in a market where efficiency is closely watched.
Harding noted that local competition loomed for Manitoba Telecom this year and that most observers expected it to relinquish a few points of its market share.

Long-distance competition may also heat up. Equal access, a system under which customers to competitive long-distance carriers can dial a number without adding a lengthy access code, came to Manitoba a year later than other Canadian provinces.

Many competitive long-distance carriers tackled the large markets of Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver before taking on relatively small Winnipeg. But Winnipeg is becoming more important to resellers and competitive carriers.
Traders see the stock as a very attractive instrument for retail investors keen on income.
"It's an exceptional deal from the yield point of view for the retail investor," said one stock trader.
"We knew it was going to open up about here," he added.
Saskatchewan's SaskTel is now the last remaining provincially owned telephone company.
